pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `go run .` and `go build .`? When would you use each?
expected_points: go run compiles and executes, discarding the binary — good during development
go build produces a binary on disk you can run again or ship

questions.prompt: Explain what each of these three lines does: `package main`, `import "fmt"`, `func main()`.
expected_points: package main marks an executable program
import makes the fmt standard-library package available
func main is the entry point where execution starts and the program exits when it returns

questions.prompt: In `fmt.Println`, what does the `fmt.` part mean?
expected_points: Println lives inside the imported fmt package
package.Name is how you access anything from an imported package

questions.prompt: Why does Go ship a formatter, and why does everyone use its output unchanged?
expected_points: one canonical style ends formatting debates
every Go codebase reads the same, which helps reading others' code
editors run it automatically; gofmt -w does it manually

questions.prompt: You make a typo like `fmt.Printlnn`. When do you find out — when running, or before? Why?
expected_points: at compile time, before anything runs
the compiler checks names/types up front — contrast with interpreted languages surfacing it at runtime

questions.prompt: Why did the exercise split `Greeting` (returns a string) from `main` (prints it)?
expected_points: returning a value makes the logic testable
printing is a side effect tests can't easily observe
main stays a thin shell around tested logic
